newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish mkt keen to see McCreevy's attitude to punt.
newsitem.headline: Irish mkt keen to see McCreevy's attitude to punt.

text.p: Irish financial markets were unmoved on Friday by the widely expected appointment of the fiscally conservative Charlie McCreevy as new finance minister.

McCreevy's plans for tax and spending are well known and he is not expected to introduce any changes to the broad EMU-oriented stance of Irish economic policy but the key issue for most market players will be his attitude to the currency which has been buffeted by selling pressure in recent weeks.
"The formation of the new government contained no surprises with the new finance minister Charlie McCreevy as expected," NCB Stockbrokers said.
"He comes to the job as a devotee of fiscal prudence and is committed in government to a targeted limit for current spending growth of four percent for 1998."

But given current concerns about the weakness of the Irish pound and McCreevy's ultimate responsibility for exchange rate policy, the immediate focus will be on his attitude to the currency, analysts said.
"The interesting question is what the government policy will be on the punt - revaluation or not?," Riada Stockbrokers wondered.
Views among economists are mixed on whether the new government will adjust the punt's exchange rate in the ERM to discourage recent speculative selling of the Irish unit.
The selling has been fuelled by the view that currencies will enter the euro at their ERM central parity and the Irish pound is currently trading well above that level.
Most analysts believe the new government will be reluctant to upset exporters and farmers, two lobby groups who argue strongly against revaluing the punt.

"I think it would be very difficult for the new government to muster support for a revaluation. It is a minority government and they are relying for support on Independents, many of whom are from rural areas with a strong farmer support base," one trader said.
Analysts also believe McCreevy will be reluctant to revalue as it would leave the Irish economy very vulnerable to a downward move by sterling at a later date.

"Given the desire of the incoming government to protect the economy if the UK stays out (of the single currency), an early revaluation seems unlikely," AIB Group Treasury's bond unit said in a research note.
But NCB believes a revaluation could be a possibility.
"We believe both the Department of Finance and the Central Bank will be urging him to revalue," it said.
By 0930 GMT, the Irish pound was at 0.9080 sterling against 0.9073 at Thursday's close. It stood at 2.6134 marks against 2.6122 at the close.
"It's pretty quiet. We're really trading off the majors," said one forex dealer, noting that the approach of the end of the quarter was depressing activity.
Irish government bond prices were a shade easier, mirroring the performance in European peripheral markets generally.
By 0830 GMT, the 10-year benchmark bond was at 109.93 to yield 6.52 against 110.00 at the close while five-year paper slipped five pence to 102.05 to yield 5.93.
Bond dealers said there was no response to McCreevy's appointment although the market was pleased with his plans to rein in public spending.
